name: Living Out of a Bag: Freelancer Housing in GLMZ
author: Compiled by the Narrows Mutual Aid Network, 2199 edition
description: A practical housing guide distributed by the Narrows Mutual Aid Network, printed in runs of approximately 400 copies and circulated through freelancer-adjacent spaces including certain Narrows repair shops, the back rooms of licensed augmentation clinics, and a handful of the Gray Zone community boards. The 2199 edition is the fourth revision; the original 2195 draft was a single handwritten page. This edition reflects input from an estimated thirty-plus contributors across GLMZ's middle and lower housing tiers. Not intended as legal advice. Annotated copies with handwritten margin notes are considered more valuable than clean copies.
body:
LIVING OUT OF A BAG
Freelancer Housing in the GLMZ, 2199 Edition
Compiled by the Narrows Mutual Aid Network

This guide exists because nobody else is going to write it. Corporate residential services require proof of employment contract. Arcturus Civil Security will flag you for extended temporary registration lapses. Your broker doesn't care where you sleep. So: here is what we know, gathered from people who have been doing this for years and are still alive.

This is not comprehensive. Update your own copy. Cross out what's wrong. Add what we missed.

---

PART ONE: SHORT-TERM HOUSING WITHOUT ID VERIFICATION

The formal rental market is closed to most freelancers. You know this already. What you may not know is how large the informal market actually is.

The Narrows — specifically the Holt Corridor between Stanchion 14 and the old Ferryman terminal — has the densest concentration of no-questions subletting in GLMZ. These are units being illegally sublet by their primary leaseholders, who are themselves often operating on thin margins. Rates run Φ180–Φ240 per week for a private room, sometimes less if you're willing to share. Listings circulate through physical boards at the Holt laundromats and through word of mouth at the three or four bars that cater to the trade. Do not ask for a written agreement. There isn't one. The moment you ask, you've told them you're either new or a problem.

In the the Gray Zone districts, particularly the stacked residentials around Anchor Block 7 in the lower Millside section, a different system operates. Extended-family units rent floor space and couch access for Φ60–Φ90 per week. These are not comfortable. The walls are thin and the ventilation is poor and you will share a bathroom with eight people. What you get is anonymity and a door that locks. The Millside network is largely word-of-mouth and you will need an introduction — someone who has stayed there before, who will vouch for you. This is not negotiable. They have had bad experiences.

For Canopy-adjacent work that requires you to be closer to the upper transit lines: the Vestibule District near Overpass 9 has a handful of what locals call ghost units — officially unoccupied flats that are rented on rotating informal leases. These run Φ400–Φ600 per week and are absolutely not worth it unless your job requires the address. If you are paying this, your job should be paying for it.

---

PART TWO: LANDLORDS WHO TIP OFF ARCTURUS

This section exists because three people we know were arrested in the last eighteen months after their landlords cooperated with ACS housing sweeps. ACS does not need a warrant for informal tenants. You have no lease. You are not legally present. They will take you.

Landlords tip for two reasons: money (ACS pays informant fees, reportedly Φ300–Φ500 per confirmed unlisted tenant) or fear (ACS can revoke a primary leaseholder's housing certificate for illegal subletting, which is an effective threat). Neither of these is about you specifically. It is business.

Known problem areas as of late 2198: the Draper complex in lower Holt has had two sweeps. The Suncross residential tower near Anchor Block 4 — avoid entirely, the building super has a known relationship with ACS District 7. In the Vestibule, the operator who goes by Maren Fell has burned two tenants this year. Do not rent from her regardless of how the price looks.

General indicators: a landlord who asks too many questions about your work schedule is mapping your absence. A landlord who is aggressively friendly is sometimes more dangerous than one who is cold. Trust people who come recommended through your vouching network, not people who find you.

---

PART THREE: THE GO-BAG AND THE BASE

If you are doing this right, you are never fully unpacked.

Go-bag contents — these stay with you always:
Identification documents (primary and any alternates), emergency medical kit sized for your augmentation profile, three days of medication if applicable, one change of clothes that is not work clothes, enough Φ in physical chit form to cover two weeks of floor-space housing without accessing any account, a charged and wiped burner comm, and whatever tools are small enough to matter.

What goes at your base and not in the bag:
Bulk consumables. Extra clothing. Any gear that requires maintenance rigs. Personal items that you would grieve. If you would grieve it, think hard about whether you can afford to grieve it. Some people keep nothing they would grieve. This is a legitimate choice and it costs something that isn't money.

A functional base on C/B-tier income means you are spending no more than Φ200/week on housing and you are not treating it as permanent. Rotate between two locations if you can. Never be somewhere long enough to become a fixture. Fixtures get noticed. Fixtures get swept.

---

PART FOUR: HOSPITALITY NETWORKS — ETIQUETTE AND OBLIGATION

Freelancers host other freelancers. This is not charity. It is infrastructure.

If someone puts you up: you owe them. Not money, necessarily — though money is acceptable and should be offered at a rate of Φ40–Φ60 per night for a couch, more for a private space. What you actually owe is discretion, reliability, and reciprocity. Discretion means you do not tell anyone you stayed there without permission. You do not mention the address. You do not bring other people to the space without explicit invitation. If you are being followed, you do not go there.

Reliability means you leave when you said you would leave. You leave the space in the condition you found it or better. You do not eat their food without asking. You do not use their equipment. These are small things. Violating them makes you someone who cannot be housed, which in this economy is a serious problem.

Reciprocity means that if you have a couch and someone in your network needs it, you say yes when you can say yes. The network only works because enough people maintain it. People who take and never give are eventually known and eventually excluded. The Narrows network specifically maintains an informal list. We will not describe the list in more detail than that.

---

PART FIVE: MAIL AND COMMUNICATIONS WITHOUT A FIXED ADDRESS

For physical mail: most of the Narrows repair shops and at least four cafes in the Holt Corridor will hold mail for known regulars. This is informal. You tip. You do not abuse the arrangement by receiving large volumes. Some brokers maintain dead-drop mail services as part of their fee structure — ask yours.

For registered communications requiring a fixed address: the Millside Community Resource Hub at Anchor 7 will register as a care-of address for Φ15/month. They do not verify what they are receiving or from whom. This has been useful.

BCI-linked communications are their own problem. If your comm is registered to a residential node, your location is pinging constantly. Most working freelancers at B-tier and above run a secondary unregistered relay. Setup guides for this are beyond our scope here but ask around — this is common knowledge in the trade.

---

FINAL NOTE

None of this is stable. The Holt Corridor network has been disrupted twice since we started writing these guides. Buildings get condemned. Landlords change. ACS shifts its attention. What's safe this year may not be safe next year.

The most reliable thing in this guide is not any specific address or rate. It is the principle: you stay alive through people, not places. Maintain your network. Vouch carefully. Be someone worth housing.

This guide was compiled with contributions from people who did not put their names on it for good reasons. If it helped you, help someone else.

— Narrows Mutual Aid Network, 2199
Next revision expected 2201 or sooner if things get worse.
